tbpn_example.episode_title: Dwarkesh Patel, Nadia Asparouhova, Augustus Doricko, Casey Handmer, Ishan Mukherjee, Mike Knoop; Trump pardons Milton, CoreWeave IPO winners

notes:
Research (recall): first principle = Aristotle's arche, 'the first basis from which a thing is known', a proposition not deduced from any other; Descartes' method of doubt is the modern ancestor (reduce to what cannot be doubted, then rebuild). In engineering practice the method is: reason from physics, arithmetic and material or unit costs instead of from analogy and precedent. Five beats matching the registry slots: (1) problem, the question as posed, which usually arrives already carrying an inherited answer; (2) assumption, the borrowed belief being removed, normally sourced to industry precedent, an analogy or 'everyone knows'; (3) fundamental_truth, what survives deletion of the belief, a physical law, a spot material price, an arithmetic identity or a regulatory fact; (4) constraint, the bound those truths actually force, which is the step nobody shows their working for; (5) rebuilt_solution, what becomes buildable at that bound rather than at the precedent. Classic textbook use: the battery-pack argument. Common misuse: (a) 'first principles' as a badge for any bottom-up analysis that is still reasoning by analogy one level down; (b) stopping at a truth that is itself a convention (a market wage, a regulated tariff); (c) no assumption named, so nothing is stripped and there is no before-and-after; (d) reading the derived limit as a plan rather than a floor; (e) the cheaper-same-thing error, where an incremental cost reduction on the incumbent machine is relabelled a first-principles rebuild.

Provenance line for this framework (the point of the page): the precedent being stripped away is normally a fact, because someone says it out loud ('everyone knows X costs Y'), while the fundamental truths, the limits they imply and the rebuilt solution are normally derived. That inversion (the assumption is the datum; the reasoning that deletes it is the inference) is the interesting provenance story.

Scout / example decision: chose 2025-03-28, Casey Handmer (Terraform Industries, ex-NASA JPL) at L3228-L3458. He runs the method twice in one uninterrupted answer: nuclear's cost is stripped from the regulator to the turbine island ('even if NRC didn't exist tomorrow ... it would still be the case that just the steam engine component is going to cost no less than coal'), and space-based solar is killed not on launch cost, where that argument is normally had, but on a revenue-per-watt identity taken from Starlink. Both chains carry real numbers, so the derived-limit slot is fillable rather than decorative.

Deviation from the expected provenance line, deliberate and worth a reader's attention: because the speaker is a physicist reasoning out loud, six of the fundamental truths and four of the limits are stated, so they are facts, not inferences. The TBPN example therefore runs 17 fact / 8 derived. This is the honest reading of the source and it makes the page's contrast sharper rather than weaker: with derived hidden, what remains is a complete first-principles argument that a human actually performed, and the eight derived nodes are exactly the joints he skipped (a5 the fuel-versus-machine frame inside the question, t8 the pivot that a PV cell has no heat cycle, c5 the 200x-400x land ratio he never divides, c6 that licence reform cannot move a turbine-set floor, c7 the allocation argument joining the revenue ratio to his conclusion, r4/r5/r6 the buildable readings). Recorded rather than forced: manufacturing derived nodes to hit an expected ratio would have been the worse error.

Other decisions: (1) the classic example is an original scenario written for this page following the battery-pack argument popularised by Musk in 2012, attributed in source.attribution, so every classic fact quotes a text that exists here rather than a half-remembered interview. (2) Handmer says steam engines run 'the Brayton cycle'; steam plants run Rankine. The slip does not touch his argument (his point is the irreducible cost of turbine plant), so t1's quote is kept verbatim and t1's text asserts only the turbine-cost claim, not the cycle name; why_this_episode flags it as a live example of a quoted 'fundamental truth' that needs checking rather than copying. (3) entities are restricted to names that appear in tbpn-transcripts/extractions/2025-03-28.json, so Starlink is listed but the NRC and amazon.com, which a1 names rhetorically, are not; listing a spelling absent from the extraction would create a join that resolves to nothing. (4) source_ref line ranges were re-verified token-by-token against the transcript at resume: r1 was L3306-L3316 and is actually L3306-L3314; a1, t2, a4 and edge te1 quote a single line and were written in the house L<n>-L<n> form.
